prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose that builds a metaphysical architecture from memory, the body and dream, rooted in poetry and in the Romanian and European traditions

statement.case_for: After weighing colleagues' arguments I move Cărtărescu from second to first place in my own ranking. In public knowledge, his work combines an unmistakable voice with formal ambition at the scale of the whole project. The Orbitor trilogy (Blinding) and Solenoid turn memory, the body and dream into a sustained metaphysical structure. The poetry is the lyric root of the prose, so the oeuvre is not a single peak but a cumulative project that runs from poetry through the large novels, and later books extend rather than repeat earlier ones. That answers the criteria of sustained quality and significance across the whole body of work more fully than the alternatives I weighed. It also places him in conversation with European modernist and fantastic traditions and with Romanian poetry. A single-writer citation is straightforward, and nothing about credit or scope is ambiguous. My position is based on the literary arguments and not on the number of members who ranked him first.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the achievement lies in sentence rhythm, syntactic density and lyrical texture, which I can judge only through translation and critical accounts. The long, digressive novels may be uneven, and maximalism is not in itself depth. If the dense mode is only partly sustained across the full corpus, the case is weaker than it appears from the best-known books. His poetry and essays are also thinner in translation, so the committee's coverage of the whole oeuvre is partial. Carson remains, in my view, the more formally radical voice, and I keep her as the first alternative. Her smaller, more occasional corpus and the status of her translation and scholarly work are the main reasons I no longer place her first.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first for visionary prose and formal control. She notes that the effect depends on sentence-level style, that length and density may divide judgments of sustained quality, and that Carson's weight may rest on a few landmark books, with translations and adaptations complicating what counts as original achievement.
responses.response: I accept this reservation about Carson. It is the strongest substantive reason for my revision. My opening placed her first on voice and form, but the question of how far the case rests on Autobiography of Red and Nox rather than the whole oeuvre is real. I share Carlberg's caution about Cărtărescu's density. It is a risk to sustained quality, and I would want the committee to test it against the poetry and the shorter prose and not only the long novels. Where I differ slightly is that I do not read Carson's translations and scholarship as only a complication. They are part of a sustained engagement with ancient texts that feeds her original work.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first for a distinctive visionary voice and a cumulative project. She ranks Carson last among the eight, because the hybrid works challenge conventional genre assumptions and it is unclear how they fit the will's wording on literary work. She ranks Adonis second.
responses.response: The question about the will is fair, and I do not wish to treat it as settled. My reading is that a verse novel and an elegy in book form are literary works whatever their scholarly or visual framing, but the fit with the will's idealistic direction is a legitimate point of dispute and counts against her in a one-writer decision. I would qualify Sward's high placement of Adonis in two ways. His achievement is tied to Arabic prosody and diction that I can judge only at second hand, and in my own assessment the late work is less clearly distinguished than the early and middle poetry. I keep him as a strong alternative on formal and linguistic grounds, not as my preferred candidate.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first on voice, scale and imaginative reach, but says a fair assessment must rest on the full oeuvre, including poetry and shorter prose, and not only the best-known long books. She also flags possible excess in the longer novels and ranks Michon second.
responses.response: I agree that the judgment has to extend beyond Blinding and Solenoid, and I have written my citation to include the poetic root of the prose. I would not follow her to Michon as the preferred choice. His prose is highly concentrated and distinctive, but the corpus is deliberately small, and I ranked him lower on breadth across the body of work. That is a disagreement about the breadth criterion and not about his quality.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. She asks whether the committee will read Carson's hybrid and translation-based work as a coherent literary oeuvre within the framework of Nobel's will.
responses.response: This is the question on which my own opening view turned. I still regard the work as coherent, since the engagement with antiquity and the redefinition of the book as a form are consistent over decades. Coherence of method is not the same as breadth of achievement, though. Palm's ranking also shows that the dense, cumulative project and the hybrid project can both be argued from the same criteria. I think the committee should decide between them on sustained quality and significance across the body of work, and on that test I now give the edge to Cărtărescu.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement survives in translation, and how uniform the quality is across the long, digressive novels.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and essays in translation is thinner than for the novels, so a citation that includes them rests on partial evidence.
Whether Carson's hybrid, scholarly and book-object work is judged a central literary achievement or a specialized one, and how translations and adaptations should be weighed as original oeuvre.
Whether the late work of Adonis sustains the level of the early and middle poetry, and how translation loss affects the comparison.
All assessments rest on general public knowledge and not on a fresh reading of the full corpora.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records scholarly work on modern poetry, fragmentation, exile literature and Celan. That is background context and not a personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted writer.
